title: “Help! I Need Appropriately Complex Texts for my Elementary and Middle School Students!” chool-students/
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart writes for the elementary and middle school teachers who have looked at his Articles of the Week lists and found them pitched well above their students - his articles stretch even his own ninth graders. He frames the underlying problem with Common Core Appendix A: newspaper vocabulary difficulty has held stable for fifty years while the reading demands placed on K-12 students have fallen. His answer is two free platforms, and he evaluates rather than merely lists them. NewsELA's distinguishing capability is the Lexile selector that serves any of its current, categorized articles at a chosen complexity level, though he warns that Lexile is only a quantitative measure and should never be the sole guide to whether a text is appropriately complex, and he flags the risk that a tiered business model eventually walls off the free content. ReadWorks tags each text by grade level, Lexile, domain, and skill, and attaches questions - which is exactly where his caveat lands, because that convenience invites teachers to print reams of worksheet-style articles to keep kids busy. The argument under both reviews is that kids get better at reading by reading, and that text selection is a professional judgment about a particular class and the discussions it is having, not an act of downloading.
points: The practical core is NewsELA's adjustable Lexile levels, which let one current-events article serve a mixed-ability K-8 class without the teacher rewriting anything.
Stuart's warning about Lexile is the more durable idea: it measures only quantitative complexity and must never be the only determinant of whether a text fits students.
His ReadWorks caveat generalizes into an ed-tech critique - a platform's most convenient feature, here pre-attached questions, can quietly substitute itself for instruction.
He anticipates the business-model risk in free classroom tools, predicting NewsELA will keep articles free and charge for assignment, annotation, and progress-tracking features.
The selection rule he ends on is relational rather than algorithmic: choose texts that fit your students, your class, and the debates you want them to be having.
quotes: This is because my articles are often a stretch even for my ninth graders (after all, the vocabulary difficulty of newspapers has remained stable over the last 50 years, whereas the reading demands placed on K-12 students in the same time period has decreased — see Common Core Appendix A, p.2). So what is a well-meaning K-8 teacher to do?

Below, I want to emphasize the awesomeness of two complex text resources for K-8 teachers. I've written about them before, but based on my recent interactions with a group of 5-8 grade literacy teachers, I feel the need to shout these two resources out again.

Now, keep in mind that Lexile is only a quantitative complexity measure, and, therefore, it should never be our only guide in determining whether we're giving kids appropriately complex texts (here's a heavily biased, significantly misleading, yet kind of entertaining New Republic article that rips into text complexity determinations that only consider quantitative factors). But assuming that you can easily grasp a concept that the New Republic author couldn't, it is awesome that NewsELA gives us control over the quantifiable complexity of a given article.

As you can see, each text is categorized by grade level, Lexile level, category (they call it domain), and, controversially, a skill/strategy categorization. You'll also notice that each article includes questions for students to answer.

Those two bad things are a stretch. The first one is Nit-picky with a capital N, and the second one is highly unlikely as NewsELA seems to be pursuing a tiered business model in which access to the articles will be free, while more advanced “pro” features (e.g., assigning articles to students digitally; allowing students to annotate digitally; tracking student progress) will be reserved for those with scrilla.

Here's where my big caveat with ReadWorks.org comes in: I'm afraid this site will be used by teachers to print off reams of worksheet-esque articles, poems, and stories to chuck at kids and keep them busy. Like I've said before, we need kids to read if they're actually going to get better at reading (just as badminton coaches need their badminton players to #hittheshuttlecock) — but at the same time, we must protect literacy from turning into a worksheet-driven, instruction-optional thing.

We teachers need to choose texts that fit our students, our classes, and the discussions and debates our students are currently having or that we want them to begin having. In other words, please, for the love of all that is sweet, don't use ReadWorks.org as a worksheet generator.
